name: Local-First Control Plane
problem: A control plane that delegates its own decisions to hosted services becomes unable to govern itself when the network, the vendor or the billing relationship fails; verification, policy and audit stop being properties of the repository and become properties of somebody else's uptime.
context: Engineering control planes, governance layers and verification runners that must remain auditable in constrained, offline, air-gapped or regulated environments, and that must not change behaviour silently because a third party shipped an update.
forces: Reach and integration convenience versus sovereignty over the decision surface
Determinism and reproducibility versus always-current hosted capability
Scale of hosted infrastructure versus auditability of a local artifact
Cost per operation versus cost of losing the ability to verify at all
Speed of adoption versus reversibility of the dependency
mechanism: Keep decisions, enforcement and evidence local and inspectable: policy as versioned files in the repository, verification as a local runner over the real filesystem, and the dependency floor as language/runtime built-ins. Any external capability is placed behind an explicit adapter seam, never at the root, so it can be removed without touching the decision logic. Network access becomes a declared, auditable boundary rather than an ambient assumption.
implementation_shape: EOS: `DEPENDENCY_POLICY_L0.md` fixes the floor at NODE_BUILTINS_ONLY with zero root dependencies; `scripts/verify-eos.js` runs the entire strict verification (939 checks at the current tip) offline against local files; `docs/` holds the SSOT; external tools are reachable only through documented adapters; locks such as `scripts/lib/knowledge-integrity-lock.js` are pure `node:fs`/`node:path`.
benefits: Verification runs offline, deterministically, on a fresh clone, with no credential
Governance survives vendor churn, outages and pricing changes
Every decision is diffable and reviewable in the same history as the code it governs
Removal of an external capability is a revert, not a migration
tradeoffs: Foregoes convenient hosted capabilities that would take minutes to wire
Requires hand-rolling what ecosystem packages would provide
Local runner cost grows with the check count and must itself be managed
Slower adoption of genuinely better external tools
risks: Local-first can harden into local-only and reject capabilities that are safe behind an adapter
Hand-rolled replacements can be less correct than reviewed upstream libraries
The check count can become a complexity budget of its own, encouraging noise over signal
anti_patterns: Making the control plane depend on a hosted service for its own policy evaluation
adoption_conditions: Root dependency count is zero and enforced, not aspirational
The full verification suite passes with the network disabled
Every external capability sits behind an adapter seam with a documented removal path
evidence: Attested as the EOS operating pattern by RSC-0003, RSC-0004, RSC-0005, RSC-0006, RSC-0007, RSC-0008, RSC-0009, RSC-0010, RSC-0011, RSC-0012 and RSC-0013.
Implemented and enforced: `DEPENDENCY_POLICY_L0.md` (NODE_BUILTINS_ONLY, no root dependencies) plus `scripts/verify-eos.js` under `--strict`.
Locally observed: strict verification completes offline on a shallow clone; see EVD-0073 through EVD-0077.

CONFLICT RECORDED: RSC-0001 cites PAT-0003 under a different title ('Non-Destructive Topic Upsert Key'). Eleven records attest this name; the single outlier is treated as a mis-numbered citation in the source record, not as an alias. Resolution belongs to a reviewed change of RSC-0001.
